documents.abstract: Purpose. This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into information literacy training in university libraries, focusing on how AI can foster critical thinking and ethical awareness among students and staff. Methods. The research employed a qualitative descriptive approach with data collected through interviews, observations, and documentation at the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing Library of Gadjah Mada University. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns in participants' experiences and in librarians' roles as facilitators. Findings. The training model consisted of three main components: introducing AI concepts and ethical considerations, practicing the use of generative AI tools for literature searching, summarisation, and academic writing, and critically evaluating AI outputs. The training enhanced participants' ability to locate relevant sources, generate summaries, and support administrative tasks. It also highlighted challenges, including difficulties in formulating effective prompts and the need for librarians to upgrade their AI competencies continually. The findings show that AI-based literacy training not only improves technical proficiency but also nurtures reflective and critical engagement with digital tools. Implications. The study concludes that AI-driven information literacy programs in academic libraries can serve as an innovative model for strengthening users' critical thinking, ethical responsibility, and digital literacy. Sustained librarian capacity-building and continuous training are essential to maximize the long-term benefits of AI integration in academic information services.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used to produce images of places, yet how users negotiate representations of real locations remains understudied. Building on the tourist gaze, we propose the AI gaze: a technologically mediated way of seeing place that is co-produced through negotiation between users and the socio-technical assemblage underlying GAI. Combining semantic image analysis, interviews, and 523 prompts from 36 participants in Poznań and Birmingham, we show that these images reinforce stereotypical tropes, lack diversity, and include visual glitches. We argue that the AI gaze is distinct because of how agency is distributed: the GAI-assemblage seemingly resists attempts to align images with human understandings of place, while also enabling users to remix and challenge stereotypes.

Is the market for human AI training work growing, week by week? This paper reports the answer measured from the public job boards of the platforms that pay people to produce human data for AI models, read daily by AITraining.jobs. From 3 Aug 2026 to 11 Oct 2026, open AI training roles on the platforms tracked throughout went up 10.5% (index 110.5); platforms listed 232 new roles in the last week and the advertised median stood at $55/hr. The analysis covers 3 Aug 2026 to 11 Oct 2026 and presents 5 tables and 4 findings; every figure carries its sample and is updated on the live report at https://aitraining.jobs/research/ai-training-jobs-index. Live report: https://aitraining.jobs/research/ai-training-jobs-index

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing not only the technological content of work but also the allocation of decision rights, the distribution of productivity gains, and organisations’ capacity to verify their own outputs. Existing literatures establish that AI can raise task productivity, algorithmic management can intensify control, and automation can alter labour shares. Few models integrate these mechanisms in one tractable analytical framework. This article introduces the bargaining-verification trap, a conditional regime in which greater AI delegation initially increases joint economic surplus but simultaneously reduces workers’ effective bargaining share, raises the congestion cost of human verification, and may erode the skills needed for intervention. We develop a two-sided model linking delegation intensity, queueing-based verification capacity, an opacity-sensitive bargaining rule, and a dynamic stock of human agency capital. We derive conditions under which worker remuneration falls while joint surplus rises; the firm’s preferred delegation exceeds the surplus-maximising level; and verification becomes less stable because review arrivals increase while independent human capacity deteriorates. A fully hypothetical numerical example separates the worker-income optimum, the joint-surplus optimum, and the firm-profit optimum. The theory is reconciled with divergent 2025-2026 labour-market evidence and translated into falsifiable propositions, measurement protocols, and governance principles. Its central implication is conditional rather than technologically deterministic: AI-mediated work can be both productive and inclusive when bargaining institutions, verification investment, and skill reproduction develop alongside automation, but increasing throughput cannot, by itself, establish that they have done so.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly encompassing industries and systems of governance, increasing efficiency, automation, and innovation. It has become a vital tool for creating text, images, music, software, and potentially patentable inventions. This rapid advancement in IP is not without risks at every stage of the innovation cycle. Traditional IP regimes arise from human creativity and invention, while AI performs activities traditionally attributed to both. India doesn't have any regulatory framework on AI-generated intellectual property, yet the Copyright Act, 1957, and Patents Act, 1970, contain certain principles—an answer to several emerging questions. This article argues that India should adopt a balanced approach to AI-generated creations instead of granting independent IP rights or prohibiting them. Instead, it should adopt a model that will protect creative human contribution as well as hold AI developers accountable for unlawful acquisition and exploitation of protected works.

documents.abstract: This technofidele and political-scientific essay deconstructs how generative AI infrastructure weaponizes human vulnerabilities for mass behavioral manipulation. documents.abstract: Digital leadership is defined as the leader developing their skills in line with technology, spreading them throughout the organizational culture, and ensuring technological sustainability. Artificial intelligence, on the other hand, is a set of intelligent systems that analyze employee behavior, communication, and decision-making processes in detail and enable performance interaction in many areas. The effect of these two concepts on organizational behavior is a critical issue that needs to be revealed in today's technological age. In line with this importance, CEO statements, considered to be decisive in determining strategic processes, were selected as the sample for the research, and a qualitative research method was adopted. Within the scope of the research, 19 videos obtained from YouTube were subjected to content analysis, and the data were analyzed using the MAXQDA 20 software. The relevant analyses resulted in 51 quotes (codes), 2 main themes, and 7 sub-themes. The research found that digital leadership and artificial intelligence are not merely technological elements but also important actors that shape employee behavior within the framework of many variables, such as motivation and commitment. This finding indicates that future organizational behavior models will be shaped by a holistic transformation within the framework of technology, culture, vision, and participatory governance. In this regard, it is considered that the research fills an important gap in existing literature by systematically addressing the effects of digital leadership and artificial intelligence on organizational behavior from a top management perspective and may provide guidance for future research.

This study employed a quantitative associative approach with descriptive and verificative methods. The population consisted of 152 employees at Pertamina Regional 4 Zone 11 Field Cepu, and a sample of 60 respondents was selected using simple random sampling based on Slovin’s formula with a 10% margin of error. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using IBM SPSS 25, covering validity and reliability tests, classical assumption tests, simple linear regression, multiple linear regression, t-test, an F-test, and the coefficient of determination (R2). The results show that safety culture, management commitment, and OHS program effectiveness were all in the very good category, with mean scores of 4.60, 4.55, and 4.55, respectively. Hypothesis testing confirmed that safety culture has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₁ accepted; p = 0.000; R2 = 41.4). Management commitment also has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₂ accepted; p = 0.012; R2 = 68.2). Simultaneously, safety culture and management commitment have a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₃ accepted; F count = 61.667 > F table= 3.16; sig = 0.000; R2 = 91.9%). The multiple regression equation obtained was Y = 24.619 + 0.783X1 + 1.111X2. Management commitment exerts a relatively stronger influence than safety culture on OHS program effectiveness. In conclusion, strengthening safety culture and management commitment is essential for improving OHS program effectiveness at CPP Gundih toward the sustainable achievement of zero-accident and zero-fatality targets.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract Purpose: This study explores the impact of the four elements of transformational leadership—idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration—on the three facets of employee engagement—cognitive, emotional, and physical—among middle managers and non-managerial employees in Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and Customer Experience (CX) organizations in Egypt that have experienced mergers or acquisitions. Design/methodology/approach: A structured questionnaire was used in a quantitative, cross-sectional study design. Transformational leadership was assessed through the dimensions of the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, while employee engagement was measured using Kahn's cognitive, emotional, and physical dimensions on a five-point Likert scale. The study collected 143 valid responses from full-time, middle managers and non-managerial BPO/CX employees with direct experience of mergers or acquisitions. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha for reliability, Spearman's rank-order correlation, and simple linear regression to test twelve hypothesized relationships. Findings: All twelve hypothesized relationships were statistically significant and positive (p < .001). Emotional engagement showed the strongest association with transformational leadership. Idealized influence had the most powerful link with emotional engagement (β = .470, R² = .221), followed by intellectual stimulation (β = .444, R² = .197), individualized consideration (β = .431, R² = .186), and idealized influence (β = .426, R² = .182). Cognitive engagement exhibited the weakest, yet still significant, relationships with all four leadership dimensions. Originality/value: This research advances the understanding of transformational leadership and employee engagement by evaluating both constructs at the dimension level instead of treating them as composite variables. It uniquely situates the study within the post-merger and acquisition context of Egypt's rapidly growing BPO/CX sector, which has received limited empirical focus despite its high consolidation activity. Paper type: Research paper. Keywords: Transformational Leadership, Employee Engagement, Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration, Mergers and Acquisitions, Business Process Outsourcing, Customer Experience.

Abstract Web-grounded artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on online information to retrieve evidence, generate answers, and support knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet the web is neither a stable archive nor a uniformly trustworthy evidentiary environment. Sources may disappear, change without notice, become inaccessible, or be deliberately manipulated. These conditions create an epistemic vulnerability that extends beyond model-level errors: even a capable system may produce unreliable conclusions when the evidence available to it is incomplete, altered, or inauthentic. This paper develops a multidisciplinary narrative review of three interrelated vulnerabilities: link rot and content drift, selective information disappearance, and source spoofing or data manipulation. Drawing on research in digital preservation, information science, cybersecurity, political communication, and social epistemology, it examines how changes in the availability and integrity of online evidence can affect web-grounded AI systems. Existing research documents substantial rates of digital decay and demonstrates the feasibility of certain attacks on web-scale training datasets. However, these findings do not establish the prevalence or coordinated deployment of comparable attacks against contemporary AI search and retrieval systems. The paper distinguishes source unavailability from source falsity, and technical susceptibility from demonstrated exploitation. It argues that epistemic reliability should be evaluated not only in terms of answer accuracy, but also through the availability, authenticity, temporal stability, and traceability of the evidence supporting an answer. It proposes a research agenda centered on source provenance, temporal verification, archival preservation, retrieval integrity, and systematic testing of how source changes affect generated outputs. The central claim is that the reliability of web-grounded AI depends partly on the survival and integrity of its evidentiary environment, not solely on the capabilities of the model processing it. Keywords: web-grounded AI; link rot; content drift; source spoofing; data poisoning; retrieval-augmented generation; epistemic reliability; digital preservation Disclaimer This paper presents a multidisciplinary narrative review and a conceptual framework for examining the epistemic vulnerabilities of web-grounded artificial intelligence. It does not claim that the prospective scenarios discussed have occurred at scale, that source disappearance necessarily indicates deliberate manipulation, or that any specific organization is responsible for coordinated interference. Throughout the text, demonstrated technical vulnerabilities, reported cases, theoretical risks, and proposed safeguards are strictly distinguished. Furthermore, the psychological literature is utilized to contextualize potential effects on memory and reasoning, rather than to establish a direct causal relationship between web instability and individual or collective memory distortion. Accordingly, the claims concerning downstream effects on AI-generated knowledge should be understood as foundational research questions that require further empirical validation. Author’s Note This paper examines the evidentiary instability of the online environment on which web-grounded artificial intelligence partly depends. It brings together research on link rot, content drift, source impersonation, selective information removal, and data manipulation to examine how changes in accessible evidence may affect the reliability and later verifiability of AI-generated claims. The argument does not assume a coordinated campaign by any particular corporation, government, or other actor. Source disappearance, content revision, ordinary technical failure, institutional decisions, and deliberate manipulation are distinct processes that may produce superficially similar outcomes. None, by itself, establishes malicious intent or demonstrates that an AI-generated error resulted from external interference. Claims about intent, prevalence, and causation require evidence beyond the observation of a missing, altered, or inconsistent source. Research on human memory provides a relevant but limited point of comparison. Studies of misinformation and its continued influence show that inaccurate information can affect later recollection and reasoning under particular conditions (Loftus, 1992; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020). These findings do not establish that the disappearance of digital sources necessarily distorts memory, that inaccessible records cause people to accept false accounts, or that such effects occur uniformly. The relationship between source instability, individual recollection, and the reconstruction of shared accounts remains an empirical question. The paper’s narrower purpose is to make the evidentiary dependencies of web-grounded AI more explicit. A plausible or even currently accurate answer is not necessarily one whose supporting evidence can be independently recovered and checked later. Evaluating reliability therefore requires attention not only to answer quality, but also to source availability, content integrity, provenance, and the possibility of reconstructing the evidentiary path. The proposed safeguards and evaluation framework are research directions rather than established solutions. The aim is to make claims about evidence loss testable without presuming either systematic manipulation or inevitable failure.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, has rapidly transformed education by providing immediate information, personalized learning support, academic writing assistance, language learning opportunities, and research support. However, growing concerns exist regarding excessive reliance on AI-generated content and its potential effects on cognitive development. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on the educational benefits and cognitive risks associated with ChatGPT using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, PubMed, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2022 and June 2026. Following systematic screening, eligibility assessment, and quality appraisal, 27 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Five major themes emerged: educational benefits, cognitive offloading, critical thinking, creativity, and teacher perspectives. Findings indicate that ChatGPT supports personalized learning, feedback, academic writing, language learning, coding, and research productivity. Conversely, excessive dependence may contribute to cognitive offloading, weaker memory retention, reduced analytical reasoning and critical thinking, superficial learning, diminished creativity, and academic integrity concerns. Teacher guidance and ethical AI practices are essential for safeguarding cognitive development. The review concludes that ChatGPT should enhance rather than replace students’ cognitive activities, supporting critical thinking, creativity, ethical responsibility, and lifelong learning.

documents.abstract: Safely overseeing AI is increasingly challenging for the humans doing it, as they must evaluate longer and more complex outputs with every new model generation. To mitigate this challenge, we could leverage complementarity: where humans and models make different mistakes, combining their judgements could yield an oversight signal stronger than either produces alone. We study this opportunity in realistic, safety-relevant settings, contributing the largest known suite of such tasks (3,957 instances across 8 datasets and 6 domains) as well as a platform and data pipeline for measuring human, AI, and human-AI performance on matched items. We collected 35,613 judgements from 416 human raters, finding a considerable opportunity for a complementarity effect. We also found that with the assistance methods we tested, human raters corrected the AI's errors less often, even when overall human accuracy rose, and the hybridisation methods we tested added little over the better single source on average. While complementarity is an important and feasible engineering target for safe oversight, achieving it remains an open challenge for future work.

documents.abstract: This paper considers key transformational processes occurring in programming and software development training under the influence of generative artificial intelligence. Based on a series of interviews with junior students, a behavioral pattern leading to degrading skills of algorithmic thinking and problem decomposition is identified. A quantitative analysis of undergraduate theses from the Institute of Information Technology and Intelligent Systems (ITIS) at Kazan Federal University (KFU) over the past three years demonstrated a significant increase in AI usage in project work and the independent development of skills for utilizing LLMs in professional practice. The drawbacks of the uncontrolled use of generative AI in the educational process and the need to develop sustainable competence in using these tools in professional software development activities are shown. A three-tiered solution is proposed: improving assessment through analysis of the process and style of coding; regulating the use of LLM in project activities and final theses with an emphasis on assessing applicability of AI; and integrating AI tools into teacher work to update content and provide feedback. The proposed approaches have both conceptual and practiceoriented nature and aim to transform the process of training software developers in the context of the widespread adoption of AI tools in IT-industry.

BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare education, research, and clinical practice.However, data regarding AI utilization patterns among doctors in Bangladesh remain limited.This pilot survey aimed to evaluate the frequency, applications, perceived benefits, and concerns regarding AI use among Bangladeshi doctors. MethodologyA cross-sectional, internet-based pilot survey was conducted among Bangladeshi doctors.Participants were asked about demographic characteristics; frequency of AI use; preferred AI platforms; applications in medical learning, research, and clinical practice; and their perceptions regarding the future role of AI in medical science.Data from 58 respondents were analyzed using descriptive statistics. ResultsAmong 58 respondents, 51.7% were female, and 48.3% were male.Most participants belonged to the 25-34year age group (62.0%), and most were postgraduate trainees (72.4%).ChatGPT was the most frequently used AI platform, reported by 93.1% of respondents.AI was commonly used for literature review (62.1%), protocol writing (58.6%), and symptom analysis (60.3%).Most respondents reported that AI improved medical learning, research, and clinical practice.However, only a minority reported frequent AI dependence in clinical practice.Many doctors also believe AI may replace doctors in the future. ConclusionsAI adoption among Bangladeshi doctors is increasing, particularly for educational and research purposes.While doctors recognize the potential benefits of AI, cautious integration with appropriate training and ethical considerations is necessary.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Student feedback is a critical input for continuous improvement in higher education, yet traditional end-of-semester written surveys suffer from low response rates, superficial answers, satisficing, and limited actionability. Voice-based conversational AI agents can conduct structured interviews at scale, asking open-ended questions and probing follow-ups, and may capture richer qualitative feedback than written instruments. This research proposal asks what characteristics, depth, and strategic value feedback collected through voice-based conversational AI agents has in higher education, and whether such agents elicit detailed, honest, and actionable feedback that can support instructional improvement and institutional learning. Drawing on survey-mode-effects research, the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, and dynamic capabilities theory, we develop three hypotheses on elaboration, social presence and disclosure, and actionability. A completed technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich established the feasibility of telephone-based AI interviews; the main field study is planned for the "Advanced Leadership Communication" course at MIT Sloan with approximately 60 students, using a convergent mixed-methods design and a four-dimensional coding framework for actionability (specificity, thematic richness, constructive orientation, contextual depth). The study extends CASA theory to evaluative educational settings, characterizes voice-based AI as a distinct feedback modality, and links micro-level feedback quality to institutional sensing capabilities.

AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: People may complete a learning programme ready to improve their practice, then return to competing priorities, established routines and uncertainty about what they can change. Who helps them interpret what they have learned and take an appropriate next step? This whitepaper examines how preparation, workplace application and further learning connect. Drawing on training-transfer and workplace-learning research, it explores contextualisation, the contributions of managers and colleagues, opportunities to practise, feedback and situations requiring work redesign. It also considers application in human–AI work, distinguishing the quality of supported performance from evidence of developing human understanding. Capability Design, Capability Leadership and Human Judgement Assurance provide organising perspectives for examining how learning and work arrangements contribute to dependable organisational capability. Proposed inquiry approaches are distinguished from established research findings. Written for organisational leaders, HR and L&D professionals, adult educators and training providers, the paper offers a practical starting point: select one consequential workflow linked to a learning initiative, clarify the intended improvement and support arrangements, and review what happens over time. This publication is CEW-FOWO-12 in the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series, Future of Work & Organisation.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

This article examines the key areas and mechanisms for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into the education system of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the context of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.Particular attention is paid to the analysis of the "Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy for 2025-2028" as an interdepartmental action plan aimed at digitally transforming the country's socioeconomic sphere and ensuring its technological sovereignty.The author examines the comprehensive modernization of the educational vertical, including didactic, competency-based, and managerial components.Using the example of the international intensive program "IT SkillSprint", launched in partnership with the global school Ironhack, the author demonstrates effective models of public-private and academic collaboration for training elite IT professionals.The paper also addresses the current status of and barriers to the development of distance and hybrid learning at the country's universities, emphasizing the need to improve the relevant regulatory framework.It summarizes the key risks associated with the introduction of AI into the educational environment and proposes systemic measures to ensure ethical and legal protection, cybersecurity, and the development of a new digital culture of data-driven management.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: Given the complex multi-trade operations, high-density layouts, and synergistic hazards with catastrophic potential in machining workshops, risk assessment demands urgent attention. Critical research gaps remain, particularly in dynamic risk assessment based on continuously updated monitoring data. To address existing challenges, an innovative method is proposed to identify, analyze, and evaluate three distinct types of risk by continuously updating both the probability and consequence based on visual and environmental data. In a case study conducted in a machining workshop, a deep learning-based method was employed to detect 13 types of unsafe behaviors and 8 types of unsafe conditions. The identification results were then input into the Signal Layer of a 31-node Bayesian network (BN) for risk analysis. Risk evaluation was subsequently conducted based on a risk matrix. The method was validated using nine representative scenarios, and the YOLOv11 model (selected for its superior balance between detection accuracy and inference speed) demonstrated excellent detection performance, with most precision scores exceeding 0.9. Even for difficult small targets, the precision reached 0.87 or higher. Both recall rates and F1 scores consistently exceeded 0.8. The risk analysis and evaluation results show that the co-occurrence of unsafe behaviors or hazards exerts a synergistic effect; even two concurrent hazards can at least double the baseline level of one risk factor. Overall, this integrated approach provides a strong framework for risk assessment in machining workshops, effectively enhancing operational safety and mitigating potential hazards.

Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used to explain concepts, support research, and provide individualized learning assistance. Its growing presence raises questions about independent reasoning, creativity, verification, and equitable access. This exploratory cross-sectional survey examined respondents? reported AI use, perceived educational benefits, and cognitive abilities they considered important to protect. A total of 66 respondents participated in this exploratory cross-sectional survey, which combined descriptive quantitative analysis with summaries of open-ended responses. Sixty-four respondents (97.0%) reported using ChatGPT or a similar AI assistant. Personalized learning was selected as an expected benefit by 50 (75.8%), while 48 (72.7%) identified understanding difficult concepts as an AI use or benefit. Critical thinking was the most frequently selected cognitive skill to protect (55; 83.3%), followed by creativity (52; 78.8%), problem-solving (48; 72.7%), and decision-making (47; 71.2%). Reported themes included individualized explanations, convenient information access, dependence concerns, verification, equity, and teacher guidance. Based on these findings and relevant literature, the article proposes a preliminary six-principle Future Minds Framework. The small exploratory sample and self-reported data do not support generalization or causal conclusions about cognition. Further research should evaluate the framework and examine measurable learning outcomes.

documents.abstract: Rapid technological advancement in the twenty-first century has resulted in alteration of s the relationships between humans and machines which further results in reshaping perceptions of cognition. In the current era, artificial intelligence is progressing in various domains blurring the boundaries between human and technology and reshaping the perceptions of cognition, consciousness and identity. The series Better than us explores the themes of artificial consciousness, human dependence on technology and reconfiguration of emotional and cognitive capacities. A number of studies have examined Artificial intelligence in literature, films and dramas, however limited research has explored the cognitive impacts of human dependence on artificial intelligence in the series Better Than US. Thereby using Catherin Belsey’s textual analysis model under the broader umbrella of Hayles post humanist theory the current Study aims to explore the representation of cognitive transformations in humans through artificial intelligence in the series Better Than US. The findings of the study reveal that the series Better Than Us presents artificial intelligence as a transformative force which reshapes human ethical cognition. The series transform the traditional assumption that moral judgment and authority belong exclusively to humans. The character representation of Arisa demonstrates the role of AI systems in decision making, legal interpretation, and protective actions. This results in a redistribution of ethical responsibility between humans and intelligent machine. The analysis further elucidates that human characters gradually begin to negotiate morality within technologically mediated environments where machine reasoning influences social and institutional structures. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Human-Machine relations, Posthumanism, Better Than Us.

The rapid expansion of urban air mobility calls for safe low-altitude corridor networks across complex urban airspace, where heterogeneous positioning uncertainties caused by navigation and communication errors elevate collision risk and constrain both route feasibility and network-wide connectivity. To address this issue, this study proposes a risk-informed network planning framework that integrates three-dimensional collision risk modeling with language-model-guided multi-agent learning for the construction of safe urban air corridor networks. Specifically, a three-dimensional collision risk map is first constructed by translating navigation and communication errors into spatially varying positioning uncertainty, providing a unified safety basis for route feasibility evaluation. Network construction is then formulated as a cooperative graph connectivity task on the risk map, in which multiple learning agents jointly balance route connectivity, construction cost, and accumulated collision risk through coordinated training and distributed execution. To further accelerate convergence in complex urban environments, a vision-language model interprets airspace structure and produces high-level priors that steer agents toward safer altitude regimes. A case study over the low-altitude airspace of Nanjing demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework in producing risk-compliant air corridor networks, with language-model-derived priors further reducing training effort by 50.3 %. The results support safer and more systematic air network strategies in complex urban environments, contributing to evidence-based collision risk mitigation and airspace management in the emerging urban low-altitude economy.

The complexity of today's transportation networks has made road safety, accident detection, and risk management increasingly challenging. Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) offer a technological base to enhance transportation safety by incorporating sensors, communications, data processing, and intelligent decision-making. This review discusses the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for accident detection and risk prediction in ITS by examining information sources, methodologies, accident investigation, and associated challenges. It examines the use of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, spatiotemporal modeling, and multimodal AI for accident detection, risk prediction, severity analysis, and active safety management. This review of studies suggests that collecting traffic, vehicle, road, environmental, geographical, historical, and driver-related information can improve understanding of collisions and support timely safety decisions. The review also highlights the importance of explainable and reliable AI that provides transparency, dependability, and accountability. However, the obstacles include data heterogeneity, model generalization, dynamic conditions, scalability, quick implementation, privacy considerations, security requirements, and compatible information systems. In conclusion, incorporating AI in ITS may have the power to shift road-safety management from reactive measures to data-driven approaches.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: This paper presents a conceptual review of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), autonomous agents, and multi-agent system security. It discusses key security threats, including prompt injection, excessive tool permissions, sensitive data leakage, memory poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, and cascading failures. The paper proposes a layered security framework incorporating identity management, least-privilege access, policy-controlled tool usage, secure agent communication, memory protection, monitoring, bounded autonomy, and human approval for high-impact actions. It also outlines an evaluation methodology using adversarial test cases and measurable security and performance metrics. This work aims to support the development of safer, more reliable, and secure agentic AI systems. The proposed framework is conceptual and literature-based; no prototype implementation or experimental results are claimed.

Artificial intelligence (AI) in education has largely been positioned as a child-facing tutor, conversational agent, or content-delivery system. In early childhood, this orientation warrants particular caution because executive functions, self-regulation, and social-emotional competencies develop through responsive relationships, play, embodied experience, and co-regulation with adults. This theory-informed conceptual design study addressed three questions: which developmental, pedagogical, and ethical principles should structure AI use in early childhood; how these principles can be translated into a system architecture; and what validation pathway is required before such a system can make defensible claims. Drawing on four evidence streams (executive-function and social-emotional development, ecological and embodied learning, human-centered AI ethics, and measurement and implementation science), the study proposes the Behind-the-Adult AI framework, an adult-mediated design framework initially specified for children aged 4–6 years. Six design principles were derived and operationalized in a layered architecture: brief, bounded, non-conversational digital developmental tasks generate behavioral indicators under transparent adaptation rules; a provisional, non-diagnostic profile organizes longitudinal information; and AI operates only behind the adult, synthesizing observations from center, home, and school into hypotheses for human review. A five-stage validation pathway with explicit decision gates separates design claims from evidence claims. The paper argues that developmentally responsible AI in early childhood should be evaluated not by how convincingly it replaces human interaction but by how effectively it strengthens the adults and environments surrounding the child, and it offers a transferable design heuristic for researchers, developers, and policymakers.

AI-Assisted Social Science Research: Methods, Governance and Reason Provenance is a practical research and educational resource for documenting and governing generative-AI-assisted social-science research. The resource develops a workflow for distinguishing AI-assisted proposal generation, researcher evaluation and governance, local empirical execution, adversarial challenge, manuscript revision and reason provenance. It includes reusable templates, completed worked examples drawn from the PISA research programme, guidance on claim preservation and manuscript governance, and public-release screening materials. The resource is intended to support transparent attribution and disciplined research practice rather than to prescribe a universal workflow or to provide evidence that AI-assisted research is inherently superior to human-only research.

documents.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) may support clinicians by facilitating information management, but their usability in real-world oncology practice remains understudied. This study evaluated the workflow performance of Artificial Intelligence-based First Consultation Preparation (AI-FCP), generating structured summaries from unstructured clinical documentation, co-created with end users. In a prospective single‑group pre‑post design, nine clinicians completed a person-level baseline, followed by 33 consultations with AI-FCP. Case numbers varied by clinic scheduling and enrollment timing, potentially introducing survivorship bias. Usability was evaluated using validated questionnaires and study-specific instruments. Post AI-FCP, overall perceived workload (NASA-TLX) was 28.9% lower than baseline (Hodges-Lehmann estimate difference −12.3; 95% CI –21.7 to –3.3), with self-reported average time savings of 3.26 min (SD = 2.65) per case. Preparation succeeded in 84.9% of consultations; 63.6% of summaries were complete. These exploratory findings suggest clinicians perceived lower workload and reported improved workflow efficiency with AI-FCP. Further research is needed to determine generalizability.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decisions in environments where data distributions, operational conditions, user needs, and risk levels change over time. Models that perform well during development may become unreliable after deployment because of data drift, concept drift, sensor degradation, population changes, or unexpected interactions. At the same time, predictive performance alone is insufficient for high-impact decisions: users need explanations that are understandable, relevant to the decision context, and accompanied by appropriate uncertainty information. This paper proposes an Adaptive Explainable AI (A-XAI) framework intended to integrate reliability monitoring, explanation generation, uncertainty estimation, human oversight, and controlled model adaptation within a unified lifecycle. The framework contains nine conceptual components: contextual data acquisition; data-quality, privacy, and drift assessment; prediction with uncertainty estimation; context-sensitive explanation generation; decision support and human oversight; risk-aware reliability gating; feedback and audit logging; controlled adaptation; and post-adaptation revalidation with version control. A formal decision policy is presented to connect predictive confidence, drift evidence, explanation quality, and consequence severity to actions such as automated recommendation, human review, abstention, or retraining. The paper also proposes an evaluation protocol spanning predictive performance, calibration, robustness, explanation fidelity and stability, fairness, latency, and operational outcomes. As a conceptual contribution, the framework is not presented as experimentally validated; its effectiveness must be tested in domain-specific studies using real deployment data and preregistered evaluation criteria. The proposed design offers a structured basis for developing AI systems that remain interpretable and risk-aware as real-world conditions evolve.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Can a robot's ethical reasoning be transparent without slowing it down? That is the question we set out to answer. Autonomous robots now make decisions that affect people's lives, and if we cannot understand how they decide, trust becomes a serious problem. We built a unified architecture that couples Explainable AI (XAI) with Reinforcement Learning (RL) through three connected components: a Perception Layer for situational awareness, a Decision Reasoning Layer that breaks agent utility down into measurable ethical sub-rewards (safety, fairness, and well-being), and a contrastive Explainability Engine grounded in a real-time Ethical Ledger. We tested it against Black-Box RL and two post-hoc XRL baselines (LIME and SHAP) across two simulation environments and a physical robot pilot on a TurtleBot3 platform. Our system reached 92±3% ethical alignment in simulation and 89±4% on the physical platform, beating every baseline (p < 0.01 throughout). In a controlled, IRB-approved user study (N=128), participants rated it higher on trust (4.5±0.4), understandability (4.6±0.3), and perceived safety (4.4±0.5) than the alternatives. Explanations were also fast: 4.2±0.6 ms on average, versus 18.3±2.1 ms for SHAP and 12.7±1.8 ms for LIME on the same hardware—well within real-time limits. An ablation study and sensitivity analysis back up these architectural choices.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

This study critically examines the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and copyright law by focusing on the three foundational concepts of authorship, ownership, and originality. It evaluates existing legal frameworks, judicial decisions, international developments, and scholarly opinions to determine whether current copyright principles are capable of addressing AI-generated works or whether legislative reform is required, and proposes recommendations aimed at balancing technological advancement with the protection of human creativity.

ABSTRACTThis thorough analysis examines the revolutionary significance of artificial intelligence (AI)in contemporary healthcare, stressing its development, uses, difficulties, and legalconsiderations. From its initial limits, artificial intelligence has quickly advanced to providesophisticated features like deep learning and predictive analytics. It is transformingmedication discovery, rehabilitation, treatment planning, diagnostics, and healthcaremanagement. Patient care is becoming more accurate, efficient, and personalized thanks toapplications like data-driven decision support systems, virtual care, and AI-enhancedimaging.

documents.abstract: This article is a systematic review of previously published, peer-reviewed studies; no participant-level or confidential data were generated. All materials underpinning the review are openly available in the Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23429519 under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence. The repository includes the complete search strategies, the screening and exclusion logs, the data-extraction and coding materials, the coding frameworks, the Severity, Effectiveness, ESI, and RRW scoring rubrics, and the analytic audit-trail documentation. The full texts of the included studies are not redistributed because they are copyrighted publications; they are available from their original publishers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) changes the conditions under which universities generate knowledge, organise teaching, evaluate individual achievement and justify academic awards. Its significance is not exhausted by the efficiency of automated tools or the detection of misconduct: AI unsettles the relationship among intended competence, performed intellectual work, submitted evidence and accountable educational judgement. This chapter develops a Rwanda-anchored, critically evidence-based account of responsible AI integration across curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, institutional management and external review. A purposive documentary and conceptual synthesis combines foundational scholarship, recent experimental research syntheses on learning outcomes and assessment validity with UNESCO guidance, the National AI Policy, Rwanda's data-protection law, Higher Education Council instruments and international risk-management benchmarks. It differentiates generative, predictive, adaptive and increasingly agentic applications; examines disciplinary and role-specific AI literacy; and analyses authorship, academic integrity, accessibility, bias, privacy, procurement, academic labour and technological dependence. The chapter's distinctive contribution is an evidence-traceable governance model connecting educational purpose, legitimate authority, bounded AI use, independently interpretable assessment evidence, learner protection and reviewable decisions. Practical instruments include an institutional AI governance and academic assessment integrity framework, task-level disclosure template, assessment-redesign matrix, risk-based tool appraisal and worked hypothetical evaluation. These are original professional proposals, not regulator-approved or independently validated instruments. The chapter concludes that trustworthy AI-enabled higher education requires greater, rather than diminished, human responsibility for what is taught, learned, assessed and certified.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence has moved from the margins of human resource management into its everyday machinery. Applicant tracking systems now rank candidates, chatbots answer policy questions, predictive models flag employees likely to resign, and large language models draft job descriptions and appraisal summaries. Research has grown quickly alongside this adoption, but it remains scattered across human resource management, information systems, operations research and computer science, and the regional scholarship published outside English-language journals is rarely integrated into it. This article reports a systematic review of 82 peer-reviewed studies published between January 2015 and March 2026, retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO Business Source Complete, ScienceDirect and the Russian scientific database eLIBRARY.RU, and screened following PRISMA 2020 guidance. Thematic synthesis produced six themes: recruitment and selection; learning, development and internal mobility; performance management and predictive analytics; employee experience and generative AI; determinants of adoption; and fairness, transparency and governance. Three findings stand out. First, the evidence base is heavily skewed towards recruitment, which accounts for roughly two in five studies, while compensation, industrial relations and occupational safety are barely represented. Second, reported benefits are concentrated in process efficiency, which is comparatively easy to measure, whereas claims about decision quality rest on weaker designs and shorter time horizons. Third, adoption failure is more often organisational than technical: the recurring constraints are data quality, scarce analytical skill inside the HR function, and the absence of an internal governance routine. We argue that value from AI in human resource management depends on treating it as an organisational capability rather than a procurement decision, and we set out a research agenda addressing longitudinal outcome measurement, employee justice perceptions, and evidence from emerging and transition economies. Keywords Artificial intelligence; human resource management; HR information systems; algorithmic decision-making; people analytics; systematic literature review; AI governance; algorithmic fairness

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has reshaped instructional practices, making teachers’ readiness and confidence critical considerations. This study determined the level of Grade 7 teachers’ behavioral intention towards AI integration and self-efficacy. Specifically, it described the respondents’ profile in terms of age, sex, position, educational attainment, and AI-related training; their behavioral intention based on attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control; their self-efficacy concerning student engagement, instructional strategy, and classroom management; the relationship between the two variables; and whether respondents’ profile moderates this relationship. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 185 Grade 7 teachers from the districts of Kadingilan, Damulog, Kibawe, and Dangcagan in the Division of Bukidnon, selected through universal sampling. Data were gathered using a researcher-made questionnaire. Mean, standard deviation, Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, and multiple linear regression were used for statistical treatment. Findings revealed a very high level of behavioral intention and self-efficacy among teachers, with a significant positive relationship between the two variables, further moderated by respondents’ profile, particularly position and trainings attended. The study concludes that teachers’ favorable behavioral intention toward AI strengthens their self-efficacy. It is recommended that school heads may enhance teachers’ readiness and confidence in integrating AI into instruction.

documents.abstract: As conversational artificial intelligence models become ubiquitous fixtures in professional and personal workflows, the nature of human-tool interaction has the potential to gradually shift from mechanical utility to parasocial dependency. While existing literature frequently addresses adverse events related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual deskilling, the pathopsychological sequelae of sustained AI integration remain largely unexamined. Here, we describe and preliminarily characterize the AI Assistant Syndrome, a human psychiatric construct encompassing acute chatbot-induced anxiety and mental exhaustion. This preliminary description will guide future systematic investigations to recognize, prevent, and treat this syndrome.

This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.

documents.abstract: Recent advances in computer vision, spatial computing, robotics, and embodied artificial intelligence (AI) have substantially improved machine capabilities in visual perception, navigation, spatial reasoning, and object manipulation. However, performance on structured benchmarks and controlled environments does not necessarily demonstrate equivalence to human spatial intelligence in complex real-world situations. This review examines whether current AI systems can reproduce the breadth and flexibility of human spatial and embodied intelligence, with particular emphasis on their implications for the potential replacement of humans by AI. The review synthesizes theoretical and empirical literature on human spatial cognition, embodied AI, vision-language-action models, robotics, and relevant AI capability benchmarks. The evidence is organised around four dimensions: (1) biological sensorimotor coupling and proprioception, (2) zero-shot spatial problem-solving and dynamic affordance recognition, (3) physical common-sense reasoning and adaptation, and (4) energy-efficient and context-sensitive spatial processing. Existing research indicates that AI systems have achieved considerable progress in perception, navigation, planning, and manipulation, but continue to encounter challenges involving unfamiliar environments, occlusion, uncertainty, dynamic obstacles, changing object configurations, physical interaction, long-horizon adaptation, and generalisation beyond training distributions. Human spatial intelligence, in contrast, integrates perception, proprioception, embodied experience, contextual knowledge, physical intuition, memory, and flexible real-time decision-making as an interconnected system. The reviewed evidence therefore suggests that current AI can augment and extend human spatial capabilities but cannot yet reproduce the breadth, adaptability, embodied experience, and contextual flexibility of human spatial intelligence. Spatial ability consequently represents an important dimension of human irreplaceability and supports a future paradigm of human–AI complementarity rather than complete human substitution.

Artificial general intelligence (AGI) has changed from a scientific aim to a moving goalpost of industrial AI ambitions. As far as the AI industry is concerned, it is simultaneously the most consequential invention in human history and a manageable, iterative technology. But what is AGI, aside from a future promise? This paper identifies four rhetorical registers through which AGI is defined, in the words of those giving it shape. In doing so, we base ourselves on the AI industry’s own discussions of AGI, including the 2026 India AI Impact Summit, AI companies’ blog posts, and journalistic coverage. Taken together, these source materials are treated as institutionalized performances of a collectively held sociotechnical imaginary through which AGI is stabilized and reproduced. As such, AGI is positioned as the next supposedly inevitable threshold on the road to superintelligence, imbued with the promise to solve all problems (a techno-solutionist register), bring prosperity (techno-utopian), pose an existential threat to humanity (techno-apocalyptic), and become no less than god (techno-theological). These rhetorical registers together capture AGI as an ineluctable sociotechnical imaginary, as it is being spoken into existence.

documents.abstract: Organizations are rapidly expanding their capacity to generate and process information through data, analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI), yet greater intelligence does not necessarily translate into coordinated organizational action. As AI increasingly participates in organizational decision-making, a central managerial challenge is shifting from generating information to designing systems that transform distributed intelligence into effective decisions, coordinated action, and organizational learning. This chapter introduces Decision Supply Chain, defined as the interconnected organizational system through which signals are sensed, information is interpreted, alternatives are generated and evaluated, decisions are authorized, actions are executed, and outcomes inform subsequent decisions. The concept shifts the unit of analysis from individual decisions toward the architecture and coordination of interdependent decision activities across actors, technologies, and organizational boundaries. Although represented as a chain, the Decision Supply Chain is conceptualized as a networked and recursive system incorporating feedback, interdependence, and learning. Drawing on bounded rationality (Simon, 1957), tacit knowledge (Polanyi, 1966), Organizational Information Processing Theory (Galbraith, 1974), and research on human-AI collaboration, delegation, complementarity, and task allocation (Fügener et al., 2022, 2026; Puranam, 2021; Shrestha et al., 2019), the chapter develops a framework for Decision Supply Chain Design. It proposes that the allocation, coordination, and governance of human and AI decision activities should vary according to five characteristics of the decision context: uncertainty, consequence, reversibility, frequency, and interdependence. The framework further identifies risks arising from inappropriate human-AI configurations, including misaligned optimization, erosion of tacit knowledge, diminished human agency, and weakened organizational learning. The chapter argues that advantage from AI may depend not only on superior algorithms or information-processing capacity but increasingly on an organization's ability to orchestrate complementary human and AI capabilities across interconnected decision processes. Decision Supply Chain Design therefore offers a systems-level perspective for understanding how organizations can convert AI-enabled intelligence into coordinated action and sustained organizational learning.

documents.abstract: The growth of digital assessment has intensified concerns about examination integrity, grading efficiency, fairness, and responsible artificial intelligence (AI). This study evaluates Eduvate CBT, an integrated role-based assessment ecosystem combining examination administration, AI-assisted proctoring, automated objective grading, reviewable violation evidence, and learning analytics. A four-week quantitative evaluation covered 250 undergraduate examination sessions across four computing courses, with usability data from 15 instructors and 5 administrators. At the session level, proctoring achieved 94.8% accuracy (95% CI 91.3–96.9), 94.6% precision, 96.6% recall, and an F1-score of 95.6%. Automated grading agreed with instructor consensus for 742 of 750 sampled responses (98.9%; 95% CI 97.9–99.5) and processed the cohort in under 10 s, compared with an estimated 23.1 h of manual grading. The aggregate System Usability Scale score was 87.4 (SD = 5.8; 95% CI 84.7–90.1). Analytics identified six low-performing items in algorithmic complexity, demonstrating how assessment evidence can prompt instructional review. The findings support the feasibility of the integrated workflow, although generalisability is limited by the single-institution design, absence of a competing-system control, and unavailable formal inter-rater reliability estimates.

Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has been extensively integrated into nursing and medical education, significantly transforming the academic practices of students. Nonetheless, the varying impacts of GAI on core competency development across educational stages remain ambiguous, with limited empirical evidence on hierarchical educational support needs. This study aimed to investigate the effects of GAI utilization on critical thinking, research competence, and academic integrity among Chinese nursing and medical students at undergraduate, master's, and doctoral levels, and to identify their specific needs for targeted GAI educational support. Methods This descriptive qualitative study analyzed semi‑structured interviews with 44 students (16 undergraduate, 16 master's, 12 doctoral) from a western Chinese medical university using inductive content analysis, with TAM and AI Literacy frameworks informing discussion. Results GAI usage patterns varied by academic level: undergraduates for coursework, versus postgraduates for literature reviews, experimental design, and data analysis. The dual academic impact featured enhanced critical thinking and knowledge acquisition, counterbalanced by risks of over-reliance, marginal clinical skill efficacy, and cognitive offloading—with research competency gains largely confined to postgraduates. A pronounced demand for systemic support, including teacher guidance and institutional training, pervaded all levels. Conclusion GAI differentially affects nursing/medical students' progression, warranting stage-specific support. We propose a three-stage TAM-extension model (PEOU‑driven, PU‑driven, critical‑reflective) to capture developmental trajectories, offering empirical grounds for tiered AI literacy curricula.

documents.abstract: Occupational health and safety (OHS) education in vocational high schools requires higher-order thinking skills (HOTS), yet formative assessment is often limited by delayed teacher feedback. This study examined whether generative AI-supported formative assessment using ChatGPT and Gemini improved HOTS and learning motivation compared with conventional teacher-led assessment, and explored the relationship between perceptions of AI-assisted assessment, motivation, and HOTS. A posttest-only nonequivalent control group quasi-experimental design involved 60 Grade X Machining Engineering students at SMK Negeri 1 Padang, divided into two intact classes of 30 students each. HOTS was measured using a 20-item reasoned multiple-choice test covering Bloom’s cognitive levels C4–C6, while motivation and perceptions of AI-assisted assessment were measured using validated questionnaires. Independent-samples t-tests were used for the primary analysis, followed by exploratory partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) in the experimental group. No significant differences were found between the AI-assisted and conventional assessment groups in HOTS scores (81.73 vs. 80.87, p = .417, d = 0.21) or motivation (54.03 vs. 54.83, p = .497, d = −0.18). Within the experimental group, perceptions of AI-assisted assessment were positively associated with motivation (β = 0.743, p < .001), and motivation was positively associated with HOTS (β = 0.476, p = .023). Although the indirect effect was statistically significant (β = 0.354, p = .042), its bias-corrected confidence interval included zero, making the mediation evidence inconclusive. These findings do not demonstrate that AI-assisted formative assessment improves HOTS or motivation beyond conventional teacher feedback. However, the observed motivational relationships warrant further investigation using larger samples, baseline measurements, and longer interventions.

Low back injuries are common among commercial fishermen and have been linked to physically demanding tasks involved in fishing operations. Occupational back-support exoskeletons (BSEs) may help reduce low back physical demands, but their effectiveness in commercial fishing has not been well studied. This study evaluated the effects of two passive BSEs on muscle activity and joint kinematics in 20 male participants performing simulated crab sorting and pot handling tasks with and without two rigid BSEs. Results showed that both BSEs significantly reduced erector spinae muscle activity, with larger reductions during crab sorting than during pot handling. BSE use also led to some unintended changes in abdominal and leg muscle activity and joint kinematics, depending on the task and device used. These findings suggest that BSEs may help reduce low back demands during commercial crabbing, while highlighting the need to further evaluate potential side effects, especially during long-term use under real-world fishing conditions.

This study emphasizes the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in aiding Omani students in the General Foundation Program to learn English as a Foreign Language (EFL). Despite the growing use of AI tools like ChatGPT, Google Translate, and Grammarly, there is limited research in Oman on learners' attitudes and the implications of AI for vocabulary instruction. A mixed-methods research design was used, and the sample comprised 151 respondents studying in the Sultanate of Oman. SPSS version 29 was used to analyze the quantitative data. The qualitative data revealed that EFL Omani students relied heavily on ChatGPT (49.7%) as the most widely used AI tool, followed by Google Translate (21.2%), Gemini AI (17.9%), Grammarly (6.6%). In addition, the trust in AI (frequency: 60), followed by cross-checking the meaning with other reliable resources (frequency: 67), learner autonomy (frequency: 67), and academic honesty (frequency: 64), but learning grammar, enhancing writing and reading skills had the lowest frequency. The quantitative data indicate an overall mean score of 3.67, suggesting a high frequency of AI tool use for vocabulary learning. The lowest mean score, 3.45, corresponds to the students' trust in the new vocabulary suggested by AI tools. In contrast, the effectiveness of AI tools received the highest mean score of 3.92. Additionally, it was found that AI tools, learners' attitudes and challenges, learning strategies, digital literacy, and how factors such as gender and academic level affect AI-assisted vocabulary learning in EFL Omani students were examined for vocabulary acquisition.

As Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) become increasingly common in modern vehicles, drivers often misunderstand how these systems work and when they reach their limits, which can lead to unsafe driving behaviors. This study examined how training modes (video vs. in-vehicle) and training styles (demonstration vs. practice) affect drivers’ ADAS knowledge improvement and decision-making accuracy when responding to system limitations. Sixty participants were assigned to one of four conditions covering three Level 1 and Level 2 ADAS features: Adaptive Cruise Control, Lane Keeping Assist, and Partial Automation. In-vehicle training produced greater knowledge gains than video-based training overall. For Partial Automation specifically, in-vehicle demonstration and video-based practice both outperformed video demonstration. However, knowledge improvement did not translate to better decision-making accuracy in any condition. These findings suggest that ADAS training should go beyond teaching system limitations and also help drivers apply that knowledge when system limitations occur during driving.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming entrepreneurship by enhancing innovation, decision-making, and operational efficiency. However, unequal access to technology, limited digital literacy, and ethical concerns constrain inclusive AI adoption, particularly among underserved entrepreneurial communities. This study systematically reviews how entrepreneurship education promotes inclusive AI adoption and supports sustainable business growth. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, the study examined literature published between 2015 and 2025 across five databases: Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink. Following screening and eligibility assessment, 54 studies were included. Findings indicate that AI literacy, adaptive learning platforms, digital mentorship, and practical business simulations can strengthen entrepreneurial competencies, innovation, and data-driven decision-making. Inclusive AI adoption is also associated with improved operational efficiency, competitiveness, and resource utilization. However, barriers include inadequate digital infrastructure, high implementation costs, algorithmic bias, and data privacy concerns. The review highlights limited evidence on long-term outcomes and environmental sustainability. Drawing on Human Capital Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Innovation Diffusion Theory, the study contributes an integrated perspective on inclusive AI, entrepreneurship education, and sustainability. It recommends inclusive curricula, ethical AI governance, accessible infrastructure, and targeted policy support to promote equitable and sustainable entrepreneurial growth.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming dermatology at a rapid pace unlike any other clinical specialty, largely because skin disease is diagnosed visually and, therefore, lends itself naturally to image-based machine learning. Convolutional neural networks now correspond with dermatologists in classifying pigmented lesions, teledermatology platforms triage patients across vast distances, and AI-enabled applications are increasingly available on patients’ screens. Yet this rapid uptake has outpaced the ethical and regulatory scaffolding needed to govern it safely. The Indian Council of Medical Research has addressed this gap conscientiously in March 2023 by publishing the Ethical Guidelines for Application of AI in Biomedical Research and Healthcare, India’s first dedicated ethics framework for medical AI. This article examines the ethical dimensions of AI in dermatology research and clinical practice through the lens of these guidelines, drawing on dermatology-specific evidence on algorithmic bias, consent, data privacy, transparency, and accountability, with recommendations for dermatologists, researchers, and ethics committees engaging with this technology.
